headline: AI agents matter most when evidence is ambiguous: TigerGraph benchmark
summary: A new benchmark shows AI agents only outperform simpler methods when data is complex and requires investigative behavior, with GraphRAG achieving 92% accuracy.
details: Everyone's building AI agents, but when do they actually provide value over simpler methods? A recent benchmark comparing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), GraphRAG, and Agentic GraphRAG on TigerGraph sought to answer this question using a dataset of Olympic event Wikipedia articles.

The benchmark tested pipelines on various question types, including simple lookups, multi-hop queries, temporal questions, aggregations, and superlatives. A key challenge was the presence of 'distractor' documents, which a plain text-retrieval system could easily be pulled toward, unlike a graph-based approach.

A standard RAG system scored 0% on aggregation and superlative questions because it couldn't accurately count events from limited retrieved documents. It also struggled with temporal questions, often selecting incorrect Olympic years due to the similarity of text snippets.

GraphRAG significantly improved performance, achieving 92% accuracy at roughly one-fifth the token cost of RAG. This approach leverages structured data from a graph database to execute queries, avoiding LLM guesswork on factual computations.

The final 8% improvement came from the agentic loop in Agentic GraphRAG, which was crucial for multi-hop questions. When faced with ambiguity, such as multiple events at a single venue on a given date, the agent could investigate and disambiguate using precise records, boosting performance from 71% to 100% on these complex queries.

The study concludes that AI agents are not universally superior. For many straightforward questions, a well-designed graph query is sufficient and more cost-effective. The agentic behavior proved its worth precisely in scenarios where evidence was ambiguous and required deeper investigation.

headline: Google Gemini app limits model access for free & AI Plus users
summary: Google is introducing new restrictions on which Gemini models free and AI Plus subscribers can access, following a recent compute-based usage change.
details: Google has begun limiting the models accessible through its Gemini app for both free users and those subscribed to AI Plus.
This change follows a previous adjustment in May that shifted Gemini's usage to a compute-based system, impacting how users interact with the AI.
While free users will face restrictions, AI Pro subscribers will reportedly gain access to the 'Deep Think' capability, suggesting a tiered access model.
The specifics of these new limitations are not fully detailed, but they indicate a move towards differentiating access based on subscription tiers and potentially usage.
